derivations.claim: For basis elements $d_{h,g},d_{k,l},d_{m,n}$, the product $(d_{h,g}d_{k,l})d_{m,n}$ is nonzero exactly when $h=gkg^{-1}$ and $h=(gl)m(gl)^{-1}$, while $d_{h,g}(d_{k,l}d_{m,n})$ is nonzero exactly when $k=lml^{-1}$ and $h=gkg^{-1}$. These conditions are equivalent since $(gl)m(gl)^{-1}=g(lml^{-1})g^{-1}$; when they hold both products equal $d_{h,gln}$. Bilinearity gives associativity on $D(G)$.

For each $d_{h,g}$, $1_Dd_{h,g}=d_{h,g}$ because only the summand $d_{h,e}$ survives, and $d_{h,g}1_D=d_{h,g}$ because exactly the summand indexed by $g^{-1}hg$ survives. Thus $1_D$ is a two-sided unit.

Both iterated coproducts of $d_{h,g}$ are $\sum_{abc=h}d_{a,g}\otimes d_{b,g}\otimes d_{c,g}$, and applying either counit to $\Delta(d_{h,g})$ leaves $d_{h,g}$, by selecting respectively the factor indexed by $e$. Hence $\Delta$ is coassociative and $\varepsilon$ is a counit. Also $\Delta(1_D)=\sum_{a,b}d_{a,e}\otimes d_{b,e}=1_D\otimes1_D$ and $\varepsilon(1_D)=1$.

For basis elements $d_{h,g},d_{k,l}$, the product $\Delta(d_{h,g})\Delta(d_{k,l})$ is zero unless $h=gkg^{-1}$. In that case its terms correspond bijectively to factorizations $rs=k$, through $(r,s)\mapsto(grg^{-1},gsg^{-1})$, and their sum is $\Delta(d_{h,gl})=\Delta(d_{h,g}d_{k,l})$. Thus $\Delta$ preserves multiplication. Moreover $\varepsilon(d_{h,g}d_{k,l})=\varepsilon(d_{h,g})\varepsilon(d_{k,l})$: both sides equal $1$ exactly when $h=k=e$.

In $m(S\otimes\mathrm{id})\Delta(d_{h,g})$, a summand indexed by $ab=h$ is nonzero exactly when $b=a^{-1}$. This is impossible unless $h=e$; if $h=e$, the resulting sum is $\sum_a d_{g^{-1}a^{-1}g,e}=1_D$. Therefore $m(S\otimes\mathrm{id})\Delta(d_{h,g})=\varepsilon(d_{h,g})1_D$.

In $m(\mathrm{id}\otimes S)\Delta(d_{h,g})$, the summand indexed by $ab=h$ is nonzero exactly when $a=b^{-1}$. Again it vanishes for $h\ne e$, and for $h=e$ it is $\sum_a d_{a,e}=1_D$. Therefore $m(\mathrm{id}\otimes S)\Delta(d_{h,g})=\varepsilon(d_{h,g})1_D$, proving the Hopf algebra assertion by [F2].

The formula in [F1] gives $(d_{h,g}^*)^*=d_{h,g}$ and $1_D^*=1_D$. On basis products, $(d_{h,g}d_{k,l})^*=d_{k,l}^*d_{h,g}^*$: both sides vanish unless $h=gkg^{-1}$, and in that case both equal $d_{l^{-1}kl,l^{-1}g^{-1}}$. Conjugate-linear extension makes $*$ an involution reversing multiplication.

The two expressions $\Delta(d_{h,g}^*)$ and $\Delta(d_{h,g})^*$ agree after the bijection $(a,b)\mapsto(g^{-1}ag,g^{-1}bg)$ between factorizations of $h$ and of $g^{-1}hg$. Also $\varepsilon(d_{h,g}^*)=\overline{\varepsilon(d_{h,g})}$. Hence the stated involution is compatible with the coproduct and counit.

In the configuration basis, each $B_f$ is diagonal with entries in $\{0,1\}$. Therefore $B_f^*=B_f$ and $B_f^2=B_f$, so every $B_f$ is an orthogonal projection.

For distinct vertices $v,w$, their gauge permutations commute: on a shared edge they act at opposite ends, as left multiplication by one group element and right multiplication by the inverse of the other, and these operations commute; on all other edges at least one action is the identity. Under a gauge change $k_u=x$ at $u=v$ and $k_u=e$ elsewhere, a face-boundary holonomy based at a vertex $u_0$ changes to $k_{u_0}H_fk_{u_0}^{-1}$: along the closed boundary walk the intermediate factors $k_u^{-1}k_u$ cancel. Each complement $I-A_v$ and $I-B_f$ is an orthogonal projection, hence positive. Their finite sum $H_\Sigma$ is positive.

For a vertex assignment $\mathbf y=(y_v)_{v\in V}\in G^V$, define the pure-gauge edge configuration $g_a=y_{s(a)}y_{t(a)}^{-1}$. derivations.claim: On the group basis of $\mathbb C[H]$, define $\lambda(h)|x\rangle=|hx\rangle$. Then $\lambda(h)\lambda(k)|x\rangle=|hkx\rangle=\lambda(hk)|x\rangle$ and $\lambda(e)=I$, so [F2] makes this a finite-dimensional representation. The regular representation is nonzero because $e\in H$. For any nonzero finite-dimensional representation, if it has no nonzero proper invariant subspace, [F3] says it is irreducible; otherwise choose such a subspace $W$ and [F1] supplies an invariant complement $U$. Both $W$ and $U$ are nonzero and have smaller dimension, so induction decomposes them into irreducibles. Applying this induction to $\mathbb C[H]$ proves that it is a finite direct sum of irreducible representations.

Let $\pi:H\to\operatorname{GL}(V)$ be any irreducible representation and choose $0\ne v\in V$. Define the linear map $\Phi:\mathbb C[H]\to V$ by $\Phi(\sum_h a_h h)=\sum_h a_h\pi(h)v$. For $k\in H$, $\Phi(k\sum_h a_hh)=\sum_h a_h\pi(kh)v=\pi(k)\Phi(\sum_h a_hh)$, so $\Phi$ is equivariant. Its image contains $v=\Phi(e)$, is invariant, and therefore equals $V$ by irreducibility. By [F1], $\ker\Phi$ has an invariant complement $W$ in $\mathbb C[H]$; then $\Phi|_W$ is onto and injective, so $W\cong V$ is an irreducible summand of $\mathbb C[H]$. Consequently every irreducible representation occurs among the finitely many summands in step 1.1.

For each irreducible representation $\pi$, choose any positive-definite inner product and average it as $\langle v,w\rangle_H:=\sum_{h\in H}\langle\pi(h)v,\pi(h)w\rangle$. This is positive definite and is $H$-invariant by reindexing the finite sum, so $\pi(h)$ is unitary and $\chi_\pi(h^{-1})=\overline{\chi_\pi(h)}$. For two irreducibles $\pi,\sigma$, define $P(T):=|H|^{-1}\sum_{h\in H}\sigma(h)T\pi(h^{-1})$ on $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb C}(V_\pi,V_\sigma)$. Reindexing gives $\sigma(k)P(T)\pi(k^{-1})=P(T)$ for every $k$, so $P(T)$ intertwines the group actions; if $T$ already intertwines, every summand equals $T$. Hence $P$ is a projection with image exactly $\operatorname{Hom}_H(V_\pi,V_\sigma)$.

The trace of $T\mapsto\sigma(h)T\pi(h^{-1})$ on $\operatorname{Hom}(V_\pi,V_\sigma)\cong V_\sigma\otimes V_\pi^*$ is $\chi_\sigma(h)\overline{\chi_\pi(h)}$, so $\operatorname{tr}P=|H|^{-1}\sum_h\chi_\sigma(h)\overline{\chi_\pi(h)}$; because $P$ is a projection on a finite-dimensional space, this trace equals $\dim\operatorname{im}P$. An intertwiner between irreducibles is either zero or an isomorphism because its kernel and image are invariant. An endomorphism of an irreducible complex representation is scalar: it has an eigenvalue $\alpha$, and $T-\alpha I$ has nonzero invariant kernel, so irreducibility forces $T-\alpha I=0$. Thus $\dim\operatorname{im}P$ is $1$ if $\pi\cong\sigma$ and $0$ otherwise, proving character orthogonality by the averaging calculation.

The character of $\lambda$ is $\chi_\lambda(e)=|H|$ and $\chi_\lambda(h)=0$ for $h\ne e$, since left multiplication by $h\ne e$ fixes no group-basis element. Define $\langle\alpha,\beta\rangle:=|H|^{-1}\sum_h\overline{\alpha(h)}\beta(h)$. If $\lambda\cong\bigoplus_\pi m_\pi\pi$ as in step 1.1, then character additivity and the orthogonality from step 3.1 give $m_\pi=\langle\chi_\pi,\chi_\lambda\rangle=|H|^{-1}\sum_h\overline{\chi_\pi(h)}\chi_\lambda(h)=\dim\pi$.
Taking dimensions of the regular decomposition yields $|H|=\dim\mathbb C[H]=\sum_\pi m_\pi\dim\pi=\sum_\pi(\dim\pi)^2$. This proves the stated formula and finiteness.

derivations.claim: In any irreducible $D(G)$-module $V$, put $p_h=\rho(d_{h,e})$ and $u_g=\rho(\sum_{r\in G}d_{r,g})$. The multiplication in [F1] gives $p_hp_k=\mathbf 1_{h=k}p_h$, $\sum_h p_h=I$, $u_gu_l=u_{gl}$, $u_gp_hu_g^{-1}=p_{ghg^{-1}}$, and $\rho(d_{h,g})=p_hu_g$. Hence $V=\bigoplus_{h\in G}V_h$ with $V_h=p_hV$, and $u_g$ maps $V_h$ isomorphically onto $V_{ghg^{-1}}$.

Conversely, fix a conjugacy class $C$, representative $c$, and irreducible representation $\pi:Z_G(c)\to\operatorname{GL}(W)$ as in [F3]–[F4]. For each $h\in C$ choose $t_h$ with $t_hct_h^{-1}=h$ and take $t_c=e$. On $M_{C,\pi}:=\bigoplus_{h\in C}W_h$ define $p_a$ as projection onto $W_a$ (zero if $a\notin C$), and define $u_g(h,w)=(ghg^{-1},\pi(t_{ghg^{-1}}^{-1}gt_h)w)$. With $h'=ghg^{-1}$, the factor $z=t_{h'}^{-1}gt_h$ centralizes $c$, since $zcz^{-1}=t_{h'}^{-1}g h g^{-1}t_{h'}=c$. For $k\in G$, the product of the two centralizer factors in $u_g u_k$ is $(t_{gkhk^{-1}g^{-1}}^{-1}g t_{khk^{-1}})(t_{khk^{-1}}^{-1}k t_h)=t_{gkhk^{-1}g^{-1}}^{-1}gk t_h$, so $u_gu_k=u_{gk}$. The fiber definition also gives $u_gp_au_g^{-1}=p_{gag^{-1}}$.

The set of $h$ for which $V_h\ne0$ is a union of conjugacy classes. For any such class $C$, the subspace $\bigoplus_{h\in C}V_h$ is invariant under every $p_a$ and $u_g$, hence under every $d_{a,g}$. Irreducibility therefore forces the support to be one conjugacy class $C$. Fix $c\in C$.

Define $\rho(d_{a,g})=p_au_g$. The identities of step 1.2 imply $\rho(d_{a,g})\rho(d_{b,l})=\mathbf 1_{a=gbg^{-1}}\rho(d_{a,gl})$, exactly the multiplication in [F1], and $\rho(1_D)=\sum_a p_a=I$. Thus $M_{C,\pi}$ is a unital $D(G)$-module. If $N$ is a nonzero invariant subspace, the projections $p_h$ decompose it into fibers because they are pairwise orthogonal and sum to $I$; $N_c$ is $\pi$-invariant, so by [F4] it is either zero or all of $W_c$. In the first case, for each $h$ the isomorphism $u_{t_h}$ carries $N_c$ onto $N_h$, so every fiber vanishes. In the second case, those images fill every fiber. Thus $N=0$ or $N=M_{C,\pi}$, proving irreducibility.

By [F3], the restrictions $u_z|_{V_c}$ for $z\in Z_G(c)$ form a finite-dimensional group representation. If it had a nonzero proper invariant subspace $W$, choose for each $h\in C$ an element $t_h$ with $t_hct_h^{-1}=h$. For $h'=ghg^{-1}$ the element $z=t_{h'}^{-1}gt_h$ satisfies $zcz^{-1}=t_{h'}^{-1}g h g^{-1}t_{h'}=c$, so $z\in Z_G(c)$. Therefore $u_g u_{t_h}W=u_{t_{h'}}u_zW\subseteq u_{t_{h'}}W$. The direct sum $\bigoplus_{h\in C}u_{t_h}W$ is invariant under every $u_g$ and $p_a$; it is nonzero, and it is proper because each $u_{t_h}$ is an isomorphism from $V_c$ to $V_h$ while $W\subsetneq V_c$. It is thus a nonzero proper $D(G)$-submodule, contradicting irreducibility. Hence $V_c$ is irreducible as a $Z_G(c)$-representation.

The constructed module has one fiber $W_h\cong W$ for each $h\in C$, so its dimension is $|C|\dim\pi$. The map $G/Z_G(c)\to C$, $gZ_G(c)\mapsto gcg^{-1}$, is well-defined and onto; equality of two conjugates implies the two representatives differ by an element of $Z_G(c)$, so it is injective. Therefore $|C||Z_G(c)|=|G|$.

For an arbitrary irreducible $V$ with support $C$, set $W=V_c$ and let $\pi$ be its centralizer action from step 3.1. The maps $u_{t_h}$ then identify each fiber $V_h$ with the constructed copy $W_h$, and the relation $u_g u_{t_h}=u_{t_{ghg^{-1}}}u_{t_{ghg^{-1}}^{-1}gt_h}$ shows that this fiberwise identification intertwines the full $D(G)$-action. Distinct classes have distinct supports; for a fixed $C$, an isomorphism restricts on the $p_c$ fiber to an isomorphism of centralizer representations. Hence the pairs $(C,[\pi])$ classify the irreducibles without duplication.

If $c'=rcr^{-1}$ is another representative of $C$, then $Z_G(c')=rZ_G(c)r^{-1}$. Sending $\pi$ to $\pi'(z')=\pi(r^{-1}z'r)$ gives a bijection of the irreducible representation classes of the two centralizers. The fiber map $u_r:V_c\to V_{c'}$ implements this relabeling because $u_{z'}u_r=u_r u_{r^{-1}z'r}$, by $u_gu_l=u_{gl}$ from step 1.1. Thus the parametrization is independent of the representative up to the stated conjugation.

The finite centralizer $Z_G(c)$ satisfies the finite-group and characteristic hypotheses of [F5], and [F6] supplies the resulting squared-dimension sum $\sum_{[\pi]\in\operatorname{Irr}_{\mathbb C}(Z_G(c))}(\dim\pi)^2=|Z_G(c)|$. Summing the squared dimensions from step 3.2 over conjugacy classes gives $\sum_C|C|^2|Z_G(c)|=\sum_C|C||G|=|G|^2$, since the conjugacy classes partition $G$. Finally, [F1] gives $\dim D(G)=|G|^2$.

derivations.claim: The group $\mathbb Z_2$ is abelian, so its two conjugacy classes are the singletons $\{e\}$ and $\{s\}$, and each centralizer is $\mathbb Z_2$. A group representation is determined by $T=\pi(s)$ with $T^2=I$. The operators $P_+=(I+T)/2$ and $P_-=(I-T)/2$ satisfy $P_+^2=P_+$, $P_-^2=P_-$, $P_+P_-=0$, and $P_++P_-=I$ by $T^2=I$; they commute with $T$, so their ranges are invariant. Irreducibility forces one range to be all of $V$ and the other zero, giving $T=I$ or $T=-I$. A scalar action on a complex vector space of dimension greater than one leaves every line invariant, so irreducibility forces dimension one. Conversely each of these two scalar actions defines a character because $(\pm1)^2=1$. Thus there are exactly the two characters $\chi_+$ and $\chi_-$ for each flux label.
By the definition of $\chi_-$, its value on the nontrivial flux is $\chi_-(s)=-1$.

The coordinate cycles $p_1,q_1$ specified in [F3] have $I=1$. Applying [F2] to their closed strings gives commutation sign $(-1)^1=-1$, equal to $\chi_-(s)$. With no crossings, $I=0$ and the string sign is $+1=\chi_-(e)$. The claim is only equality of these finite algebraic signs; it asserts no general braid representation or physical realization.
